newsitem.title: UK: British services sector flourishes in March-survey.
newsitem.headline: British services sector flourishes in March-survey.

text.p: Activity in Britain's services sector picked up pace in March with output, new and outstanding business, employment and prices all rising, a new business survey said on Thursday.

The Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply (CIPS) said its business activity index, which measures output of the service economy, recorded an expansion of activity every month since last July when the survey began, with growth accelerating sharply in March.
The index stood at a seasonally-adjusted 63.3 compared with 60.4 in February and 56.6 last July.
Indices are calculated to measure changes in business conditions, with readings above 50 indicating an expansion and below 50 a contraction.

The survey is based on responses from 500 British executives in private sector service industries, including transport and communications, financial intermediation, business services, personal services and hotel and restaurants, but excluding wholesale and retail.
Services make up around two thirds of the British economy.
"Over 35 percent of all companies reported an increase in business activity while just 9.0 percent reported a decline," CIPS said.
March also saw the largest increase in new business since the survey began. The incoming new business index rose to 62.4 percent from 60.9 in February and 57.1 percent last July.

"The growth in demand over the past nine months has generally been attributed simply to the improved economic climate, which a growing number of firms have taken advantage of through greater sales and marketing activity," CIPS said.
It said a consequence of this growth of incoming new business had been a rise in the amount of work outstanding, or work in hand, which also rose sharply in March.
But the survey found a growing number of firms have been unable to meet demand due to lack of resources -- most notably a lack of highly skilled personnel.

As firms were forced to pay up to secure staff, input costs rose in the month. CIPS said the major input cost for firms was labour and the higher input costs reflected higher wages paid in the sector.
"With the labour market continuing to tighten, rising wages and salaries were found to have been the principal cause of a further increase in costs during March," it said.
But it found that robust demand allowed firms to pass these higher costs on in higher prices. Prices charged rose for the fifth month in a row.

Looking ahead, three quarters of all companies said they expected higher activity in a year's time and only 6.0 percent saw a decline. "Such buoyant confidence has been evident for nine months running," the survey said.
